title: Complexity and Asymptotic Analysis
relevance: Interviewers and OAs use asymptotic complexity to judge whether a candidate can derive growth from code, distinguish worst/average/amortised costs, and reject algorithms that will TLE under given constraints.

phases.goal: Establish that complexity is machine-independent growth rate, and that Big-O/Omega/Theta bound that growth with the usual dropping rules.

must_hit.point: Asymptotic analysis asks how the number of elementary operations grows with input size n; it is deliberately independent of hardware, compiler, and wall-clock time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts stopwatch timing with counting comparisons/arithmetic/accesses and says complexity is about growth rate in n.

must_hit.point: f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n0 such that for all n ≥ n0, 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c · g(n) — an upper bound that need not be tight.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the existential-c-and-n0 definition and notes that 2n+5 is O(n) and also (loosely) O(n²).

must_hit.point: Big-Omega is a lower bound; Big-Theta is a tight bound meaning both O and Omega of the same g.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says Ω means grows at least as fast as a constant times g, and Θ sandwiches from above and below.

must_hit.point: For f(n) = 5n² + 100n + 7, drop lower-order terms then the leading constant to get O(n²); interviews usually mean the tightest simple upper bound.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks 5n² dominating 100n and 7, then drops the 5, and notes we usually mean tight Big-O even when we write O.

must_hit.point: For large n the ladder is O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders the common classes correctly and gives one-line intuition per rung (halving, once-through, nested pairs, subsets, permutations).

probes: What does it mean to say an algorithm is O(n), and how is that different from measuring runtime in seconds?
Is every O(n) bound tight? How do Big-Omega and Big-Theta relate?

hints.1: Think about what stays the same if you change machine or compiler.
hints.2: State the Big-O inequality with c and n0, then contrast upper vs lower vs tight.
hints.3: Growth in elementary ops vs n; O is eventually ≤ c·g; Θ is both O and Ω; drop lower terms and constants for the class.

phases.goal: Show how to read C++ control flow into a complexity class: sequential vs nested work, halving, recurrences, and extra space including recursion depth.

must_hit.point: Sequential costs add and the dominant term wins; independent nested Θ(n) loops multiply to Θ(n²), and a triangular inner bound still sums to O(n²).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says O(n)+O(n log n)=O(n log n), nested full loops give Θ(n²), and 0+1+…+(n−1)=n(n−1)/2 = O(n²).

must_hit.point: A loop that halves (or shrinks by a constant fraction) each step is O(log n); stepping by a constant like i += 2 is still O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains n/2ᵏ ≈ 1 ⇒ k ≈ log₂ n for halving, and that n/2 iterations is only a constant factor so still O(n).

must_hit.point: Merge sort satisfies T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) with T(1)=O(1); the recursion tree has Θ(log n) levels each costing cn, so T(n)=Θ(n log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes the recurrence, sketches levels summing to cn across log n levels, or uses Master-theorem intuition with a=2, b=2, d=1.

must_hit.point: Space complexity usually means extra memory beyond the input; recursion stack depth counts as space, and portable C++ must not rely on tail-call elimination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts iterative O(1) extra space max with depth-n recursion using O(n) stack, and notes merge sort’s typical O(n) buffers plus O(log n) stack.

must_hit.point: std::vector push_back is O(1) amortised: capacity doubling makes total copy work across reallocations less than n, so n pushes cost less than 2n total.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes geometric copies 1+2+4+…+n/2 < n plus n placements ⇒ < 2n total ⇒ O(1) per push across the sequence.

probes: What is the time complexity of this code? Walk the loops or recursion aloud.
How do you get O(n log n) from the merge-sort recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)?

hints.1: Identify n, then ask whether work is sequential, nested, or shrinking.
hints.2: Add sequential costs, multiply nested loops, write a recurrence for recursion, and name extra space including stack.
hints.3: Dominant term after add/multiply; halving ⇒ log n; merge-sort tree Θ(log n) levels × O(n); state extra space and that depth-n recursion is O(n) stack.

phases.goal: Separate worst/average/amortised meanings and explain when Big-O hides constants, locality, and small-n behavior.

must_hit.point: Best, average, and worst case can differ for one algorithm: quicksort is best/average O(n log n) but worst O(n²) with a naive pivot; std::sort’s introsort guarantees O(n log n) worst case.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names quicksort’s cases and that introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback) restores worst-case O(n log n).

must_hit.point: Hash tables are average O(1) lookup/insert but worst O(n) under pathological collisions; std::map/set are guaranteed O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says average O(1)/worst O(n) for unordered containers and guaranteed O(log n) for map/set.

must_hit.point: Amortised O(1) for push_back is not worst-case O(1) for a single call and is not the same as average-case over a random input distribution.
must_hit.evidence_hint: One push_back can be O(n); amortised bounds sequences of operations; average-case is probabilistic over inputs.

must_hit.point: Same asymptotic class can differ sharply in practice: constant factors, small n, and cache locality (vector vs list) can dominate wall-clock even when both are O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions 1000n vs n both O(n), small-n where n! or n² can win, and contiguous vs pointer-chasing locality.

probes: For hash maps, what complexity do you quote — and for std::map?
Is amortised O(1) the same as every push_back being O(1)?

hints.1: Ask whether the interviewer wants worst case, and whether cost is per operation or over a sequence.
hints.2: Separate single-op worst case, amortised sequence cost, and average over random inputs; then say what Big-O hides.
hints.3: unordered: avg O(1)/worst O(n); map: O(log n); one push_back may be O(n) though amortised O(1); same Big-O ≠ same wall-clock.

phases.goal: Turn constraints into a yes/no complexity budget and pick an algorithm class that fits.

must_hit.point: Rule of thumb on typical online judges: about 10⁸ simple operations per second, so design for ≲ 10⁸ elementary steps in one second.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the ~10⁸ ops/sec budget (noting judges may be closer to 10⁷–5·10⁸) and ties it to the time limit.

must_hit.point: Map input size to an affordable class: e.g. n ≤ ~10⁵–10⁶ usually allows O(n log n); n ≤ ~5000 allows O(n²); n ≤ ~20–22 allows O(2ⁿ); n ≤ ~11 allows O(n!).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the budget table qualitatively with the listed n bands and matching classes.

must_hit.point: Given n ≤ 10⁵, you need O(n log n) or better; an O(n²) approach expects ~10¹⁰ ops and will TLE.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly rejects nested O(n²) at n=10⁵ via the ~10¹⁰ estimate and accepts sort-level O(n log n).

must_hit.point: Contests for n ∼ 10⁵ are almost always fought in the O(n)–O(n log n) band; prefer the slowest class that still fits, and watch large constants (map vs unordered_map, slow I/O).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks simplest fitting class for n∼10⁵ and mentions hidden constant/I/O pitfalls.

probes: Given n ≤ 10⁵, what complexity do you need?
How do you pick an algorithm from constraints n, m, and the time limit?

hints.1: Estimate total elementary steps from n and the candidate class.
hints.2: Use the ~10⁸ ops/sec rule, then match n to the complexity ladder band.
hints.3: n≤10⁵ ⇒ O(n log n) or better; O(n²) → ~10¹⁰ → TLE; choose slowest class that still fits.

tradeoffs.topic: Amortised O(1) vs worst-case O(1) for vector push_back
tradeoffs.strong_answer: push_back is O(1) amortised over n pushes (total < 2n with doubling), but a single call may reallocate in O(n). Latency-sensitive code cannot treat amortised as every-call-fast; contest TLE cares about total work, where amortised bounds are the right tool.

tradeoffs.topic: Same Big-O class vs wall-clock (e.g. vector vs list scan)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use Big-O to reject impossible classes and compare growth families. Within one class, constants, small n, and cache locality decide: contiguous vector scans often beat pointer-chasing list/tree walks despite identical O(n).

tradeoffs.topic: unordered_map average O(1) vs map guaranteed O(log n)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Prefer unordered_map/set when average O(1) matters and adversarial hashing is not a threat; otherwise custom hash or fall back to map/set for order or guaranteed O(log n). Interviewers usually want worst-case unless they ask for average.
Always state extra space unless asked for total. Trading O(n) memory for a better time class (prefix sums, hash sets, Fenwick) is a standard move; recursion depth is part of that space cost.

gotchas.trap: Treating a loose Big-O as the algorithm’s true cost, or treating dropped constants as irrelevant to performance.
gotchas.correction: Big-O need not be tight (2n+5 is also O(n²)). Dropping constants is correct for asymptotic class but wrong as a prophecy when n is small or two algorithms share a class — e.g. 1000n and n are both O(n), and at n=10⁶ the heavier constant may TLE.

gotchas.trap: Confusing amortised, average-case, and single-operation worst-case.
gotchas.correction: Amortised is a sequence accounting guarantee (n pushes total O(n)). Average-case is expectation over an input distribution. Worst-case single push_back can still be O(n) even when amortised O(1).

gotchas.trap: Quoting only average O(1) for hash tables, or forgetting recursion uses space.
gotchas.correction: Say average O(1), worst O(n) for unordered_map/set; map/set are guaranteed O(log n). Recursion stack depth is space — depth-n recursion is O(n) stack even with O(1) locals per frame.

gotchas.trap: Assuming vector end-insert cheapness applies to middle insert/erase.
gotchas.correction: vector/string end-insert is amortised O(1); middle insert/erase is O(n). deque end ops are similarly cheap at both ends, not a license for middle edits.
